subject: AI & Agents
title: Deepfakes and Consent
description: A quick, practical guide to Deepfakes and Consent.

hook.text: A student finds a realistic fake video of herself online. She never consented. Nobody told her.

buildup.text: Deepfake technology can generate realistic images and videos of anyone from a few photos.

discovery.text: Non-consensual deepfakes disproportionately target women and are used for harassment.

twist.text: The technology is free and easy to use. Creating a deepfake takes minutes, not expertise.

climax.text: Laws are catching up. Several countries now criminalize non-consensual deepfakes.

punchline.text: Technology moved faster than consent. The law races to catch up.

quiz.question: Who are disproportionately targeted by non-consensual deepfakes?

details.summary: Deepfake technology can place anyone's face onto explicit or compromising content without their consent. Victims face reputational harm, emotional trauma, and limited legal recourse.
details.whyItMatters: Non-consensual deepfakes disproportionately target women and are a growing form of digital abuse. Stronger legal protections and detection tools are urgently needed.
takeaways: Deepfakes can create non-consensual explicit imagery of anyone
Women are disproportionately targeted by deepfake abuse
Legal frameworks are slowly catching up to the technology

faq.question: What percentage of deepfakes are non-consensual explicit content?
faq.answer: Studies estimate over 90% of deepfake videos online are non-consensual pornography, primarily targeting women. The technology has become increasingly accessible to bad actors.

faq.question: What legal protections exist against non-consensual deepfakes?
faq.answer: A growing number of jurisdictions are passing specific deepfake laws. The UK criminalized sharing intimate deepfakes in 2023, and several US states have enacted similar legislation.
